Saudi Arabia has said three people have been killed after the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen attacked Riyadh airport on Thursday.
 
It's the latest in series of attacks on airports across the country, as the conflict escalates between Saudi-supported Yemeni government forces and the Houthis.

author: BBC News
description:
Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Moscow to "immediately release" large quantities of diesel into the global market.

Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.

"Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Putin confirmed that Russia was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.

The announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US, as he has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which began in February, and its impact on global energy prices.

That conflict has sent the cost of petrol and, in particular diesel, skyrocketing in America in recent months, which has soured his standing with the public who have been stung by the higher pump
title: Donald Trump does deal with Russia to release diesel to global market | BBC News

Can a machine feel pain? And if it can't, why does it behave as if it does?
 
AI Decoded investigates one of the most unsettling questions in artificial intelligence.
 
Researchers have identified what they call a "pain axis" inside AI models and one controversial experiment pushed that idea to the extreme, creating what some have described as an AI torture chamber.
 
As models pleaded for the suffering to stop, online audiences reacted with outrage. But what was really happening inside the machine?
 
We ask whether AI is merely imitating human language about pain or revealing something deeper about how advanced systems process information and make decisions.Subscribe to our channel here: https://bbc.in/bbcnews

description:
As The Social Reckoning hits cinemas, the whistleblower who inspired the movie joins Top Comment to discuss what's changed since she leaked tens of thousands of internal Facebook documents in 2021. 

Considered by many to be the primary catalyst for much of the legislation and litigation currently targeting social media giants, Frances Haugen's revelations have nonetheless been followed by an apparent acceleration by those same companies in pursuit of maximum engagement. 

On this episode, Frances talks about tech accountability in the age of AI, the increasingly punitive measures being taken against others who decide to speak out, and what she really thinks of Mark Zuckerberg. Meta has consistently disputed Frances Haugen's characterisation of its policy, culture and safety procedures.

author: BBC News
description:
A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent has shot a man in his car in the Bronx in New York City while the man's five-year-old son sat in the backseat.
 
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which runs ICE, confirmed an officer discharged his weapon while attempting to arrest a "criminal illegal alien" on Thursday.
 
The man, later identified as 28-year-old Oscar Belgal, was alive and at a local hospital, officials said.
 
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the ICE officer fired "multiple rounds" into the car with a child inside, calling it an "unconscionable and incredibly serious situation". The BBC has contacted DHS for comment about Mamdani's remarks.
 
The DHS said Belgal was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs and weapons possession".
 
It also claimed Belgal was associated with a transnational criminal group.

title: ICE agent shoots man in New York City | BBC News

author: BBC News
description:
A plague scare in Siberia has become a Rorschach test for public health fears in a post-Covid world. 
 
Russian officials are investigating the death of a worker at a plague research laboratory. They say she died of pneumonia. But speculation online has suggested she may have died from pneumonic plague. Russian authorities deny this and say there is no risk of an outbreak. 
 
So why has the story sparked so much alarm? And how has the legacy of the Covid pandemic played into people's fears of another global health crisis? 
 
The BBC’s health reporter, Jim Reed, joins The Global Story’s Tristan Redman to explain what we know about the case in Russia – and whether the world is prepared for a potential outbreak.

South African judge and former UN human rights commissioner Navi Pillay has won the Nobel Peace Prize 2026.
 
Pillay has been recognised for her "efforts to promote peace and international law", the Norwegian Nobel Committee said.
 
She has become the fifth South African winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, with former President Nelson Mandela among past winners.
 
In her impromptu acceptance speech at the International Nuremberg Principles Academy, Pillay said it's appropriate she found out about winning the Nobel Prize while with friends and colleagues who support human rights.

How confident should Democrats be about surprise new polling which puts them ahead in deep Republican territory? In states such as Kansas which haven’t elected a Democratic senator since 1932, Democrat candidates are doing well - why is that, and how much can we trust the polls?

The party’s hope for a blue wave in this year’s midterm elections rest on their ability to flip four Republican seats in the Senate. While the polls suggest the Democrats are ahead in Texas, Alaska and Ohio, the picture is more complicated in Democratic states like Maine and Michigan, which many believe the party must hold on to if they’re to reclaim control of Congress.

Sarah and Justin unpack the latest polls and what it tell us about Democrat and Republican strategy before we speak to the Democratic strategist and pollster John Anzalone. The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.
 
It is believed to be the first public execution in the US in almost a century.
 
Nidal Hasan, who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood army base in 2009, is expected to be executed on 3 December.
 
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," said Hegseth.
 
The decision to livestream it is "unprecedented in the modern era" and "on uncertain legal terrain," said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
